activities.caption: proposition or not — file each item
activities.name: lpPropSort

config.prompt: File each item under what it is:
config.why: A proposition is a statement that is definitely true or false — the self-referencing sentence is neither, and therefore not a proposition.

activities.anchor: if pigs fly, I am the Pope
activities.caption: true or false — the vacuous promise
activities.name: lpVacuousJudge

config.statement: In logic, 'if pigs fly, I am the Pope' is a false statement, because pigs do not fly.
config.why: If the hypothesis is false, the implication is vacuously true — the promise 'Q whenever P' has never been broken, because the condition never arose.

activities.caption: pair each cousin with its status
activities.name: lpCousinMatch

config.prompt: Pair each cousin of P → Q with its logical status:

pairs.right: not equivalent — the sprinklers ran this morning
not equivalent, and equivalent to the converse
always logically equivalent to the original

config.why: Keeping the three cousins straight is half of careful reasoning — only the contrapositive says exactly what the original says.

activities.anchor: if n² is even, then n is even
activities.caption: two routes to one claim — drag the divider
activities.name: lpContrapositiveCompare

config.prompt: Proving 'if n² is even, then n is even' — drag the divider:

before.label: forwards
before.text: square an arbitrary number and inspect parity — clumsy

after.label: contrapositive
after.text: n odd means n = 2m + 1, so n² = 2(2m² + 2m) + 1 — visibly odd, one line

config.why: Sometimes the contrapositive is dramatically easier to argue — and the original claim comes free by the truth-table identity.

config.prompt: One of these claims about inference forms is wrong — click it:
lines: Affirming the consequent: 'no inverse; therefore det = 0' — invalid.
Denying the antecedent fails the same way.
The converse doing the work is what makes it illegal.
Affirming the consequent is a valid inference form.
config.correction: Affirming the consequent is invalid — the converse is doing the work, and non-invertibility might arise another way.
config.why: The inference form is still illegal, whatever the facts of the particular case.

config.text: Quantifiers behave oppositely under negation: the negation of 'all primes are odd' is 'there %%0%% a prime that is even' — and a single example (2) settles it. The negation of 'there is a largest prime' is '%%1%% prime has a bigger prime'.
config.hint: Flipping 'all' gives 'there exists'; flipping 'there exists' gives 'every'.

config.prompt: Rebuild Euclid's infinitude argument — what comes first:
items: Suppose the primes are finite: p₁ … pₙ is the complete list
Divide N by each prime: each leaves remainder 1
N is prime or has a missing factor — either way, contradiction
config.why: No new primes were computed, no formula found — a single impossible consequence demolished the assumption.

activities.anchor: the base case is a formality
activities.caption: the domino that never fell
activities.name: lpBaseBranch

config.root: A student proves the inductive step perfectly but skips the base case. What have they shown?

choices.label: The full theorem — the step is the hard part
choices.feedback: Nothing: without the base case no domino is ever tipped — the bogus 'all horses are the same colour' proof fails exactly at the jump from 1 to 2.

choices.label: Nothing yet — a working step plus a verified base is the whole theorem
choices.feedback: Right — either one alone proves nothing.

choices.label: Enough for all large n
choices.feedback: No — the step is the conditional P(k) → P(k+1); it needs a first domino to start the chain.

broken.text: A valid step for every group size except the jump from 1 to 2 is a proof of nothing.

right.text: The base case tips domino 1; the step guarantees each falling domino tips the next.

large.text: Conditionals do not fire until their antecedent does.

config.why: A working step plus a verified base is the whole theorem; either one alone proves nothing.

activities.anchor: fails at n = 41, where the value is 41²
activities.caption: call the breaking point
activities.name: lpEulerEst

config.prompt: Euler's n² − n + 41 yields a prime for every n from 1 to 40. At what n does it first fail?
config.why: At n = 41 the value is 41² — testing, however extensive, is not proof; it is suspicion with data.
config.context: no number of confirming examples proves a universal claim, but a single counterexample destroys it

activities.anchor: State the claim and the type of argument before starting
activities.caption: order the writing discipline
activities.name: lpCleanOrder

config.prompt: Order the clean-proof discipline — what comes first:
items: State the claim and the type of argument before starting
Define every variable before using it
Give each line a reason — obviousness is where errors live
config.why: The diagram proposes; only the argument disposes — every claim in a written proof must point to a justification, never to the figure.
